endorsements.quote: In healthcare, this may translate to clinician-led AI task forces, crossdepartmental working groups, and rotating specialty leadership across deployment phases.

Leaders must directly engage with frontline teams to assess whether a tool meets multiple relevant criteria including: clinical benefit, safety, technical security, cost-benefit return, relative ARTICLE IN PRESS ARTICLE IN PRESS advantage to alternative technologies, interoperability and compatibility with workflows, clinician learning curves, patient ease of use, simplicity, observability, and alignment with organizational values and priorities 20.

unlisted_practices: Align AI deployment with employees' four fundamental workplace drives (acquire, bond, comprehend, defend).
Reward clinical champions with recognition, authorship, and professional titles.
Communicate the evidentiary basis of AI interventions adequately to staff.
Align organizational artifacts, espoused values, and underlying assumptions with long-term AI adoption goals.
Reconcile the priorities of clinicians, AI developers, and executives to ensure effective AI deployment and governance.
Deliberately cultivate psychological safety in clinical teams so staff can raise AI safety concerns.
Match leadership style to the clinical deployment context (task-oriented for acute settings, relationship-oriented for patient education).
Embed clinician-leaders in units to drive AI integration.
Embed core AI competencies in physician training pipelines, such as electives, dual-degree programs, and specialty tracks.
Emphasize critical thinking and physician autonomy in AI education.
Provide protected time and incentives for clinicians engaged in AI deployment activities such as piloting, workflow redesign, integration, and training.

screen.reason: Commentary examining organizational culture and leadership frameworks to guide clinical AI deployment.
